section_summary: This section closes with a Soviet critique of Japan’s prewar constitution and the Shidehara government, followed by British assessments of the American-led occupation, the new constitution, elections, and the Yoshida cabinet. The later documents warn that Allied Council representatives were becoming involved in Japanese domestic politics and discuss British concern about William Macmahon Ball’s conduct. A London Embassy despatch then transmits Sir Paul Butler’s Manchester Guardian article, which praises parts of MacArthur’s democratization program while questioning Article 9 and the durability of imposed reforms.

people.name: A. Polesski

people.name: Higashikuni
people.role: Former Japanese prime minister whose government preceded Shidehara’s.

people.name: Kijūrō Shidehara
people.role: Japanese premier and head of the cabinet criticized in the Soviet article.

people.name: Sadamu Shimomura
people.role: Japanese Minister of War and former representative on the Entente commission overseeing German compliance with the Versailles Treaty.

people.name: Fumimaro Konoe
people.role: Prince and chairman of a commission reviewing the Japanese constitution; characterized by the Soviet article as a leading war criminal.

people.name: Sir Paul Butler
people.role: Far Eastern expert at the Royal Institute of International Affairs and author of the Manchester Guardian article.

people.name: Douglas MacArthur
people.role: Supreme Commander directing the Allied occupation and political reforms in Japan.

people.name: Shigeru Yoshida
people.role: Japanese prime minister, head of a Liberal-Progressive coalition, and former ambassador in London.

people.name: Waldemar J. Gallman
people.role: U.S. diplomat who signed the London telegrams.

people.role: British official with whom the U.S. Embassy discussed Allied Council activity in Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram 3653: Digest of “Reactionary Constitution of Japanese Militarists”
subfiles.about: Transmits a summary of A. Polesski’s Red Star attack on Japan’s constitution, ruling elite, and post-surrender resistance to democratization.
subfiles.summary: Polesski describes the Japanese constitution as a legal cover for imperial absolutism, with a weak parliament, restricted suffrage, and systematic repression of workers, dissenters, and non-Shinto believers. He argues that the Higashikuni and Shidehara governments sought to preserve the military-police system after surrender. The article criticizes Shimomura’s appointment, continued detention of political prisoners, obstruction of investigations into the Black Dragon Society, and Konoe’s constitutional commission as efforts to evade the Potsdam Declaration.

subfiles.title: Telegram 9503: Digest of Sir Paul Butler’s Article on Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Sir Paul Butler’s Manchester Guardian assessment of the occupation and democratic reconstruction of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butler considers the decision to retain the throne and govern through existing Japanese institutions broadly successful, while emphasizing that the emerging order follows an American pattern. He praises MacArthur’s political reeducation program, the first free election, and the new constitution, but doubts that Article 9 will endure once Allied coercive power recedes. He also warns against Allied Council representatives taking sides in domestic politics and against a premature revival of Japanese influence in a divided China.

subfiles.title: Telegram 9550: British Concern over Ball’s Activities in Japan
subfiles.from: Waldemar J. Gallman, U.S. Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Reports a conversation with Sargent concerning William Macmahon Ball’s involvement in Japanese internal politics.
subfiles.summary: Gallman raised the Manchester Guardian’s criticism of Allied Council representatives taking sides in Japanese politics and referred to Atcheson’s reports from Tokyo. Sargent replied that British authorities knew of and deplored Ball’s activities and had discussed the matter with Evatt. He nevertheless believed Ball’s temperament made persuasion toward a more cooperative attitude unlikely to succeed.

subfiles.title: Despatch 2681: Transmitting “Democratic Japan”
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, London, for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of the Manchester Guardian clipping summarized in telegram 9503.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy transmits the full newspaper clipping on which its November 14 telegram was based. The enclosure is identified as an article from the Manchester Guardian dated November 14, 1946, with a copy also directed to CINCAFPAC in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: “Democratic” Japan: General MacArthur’s Policy
subfiles.about: Assesses MacArthur’s occupation policy, Japan’s new political order, and the prospects for durable democracy.
subfiles.summary: Butler argues that retaining the Emperor facilitated surrender and administration while MacArthur’s reforms placed Japan on an essentially American democratic course. He reviews the Japanese Bill of Rights, the Emperor’s renunciation of divinity, the purge of militarist nationalists, the new constitution, women’s enfranchisement, and the first free election. Although praising MacArthur and noting Allied confidence in Yoshida’s coalition, he questions Article 9, observes that the purge removed capable administrators, and warns that practical democracy remains fragile and vulnerable to Allied political rivalries.
